canonical_statement: The review evaluated benefits and harms of currently marketed sodium-glucose co-transporter 2 inhibitors in adults with type 2 diabetes using systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
The quantitative synthesis included 42 randomized controlled trials reported in 59 publications, comprising 24,500 participants with type 2 diabetes.

population.label: Participants with type 2 diabetes across 42 included randomized controlled trials

canonical_statement: The search covered the Cochrane Library, MEDLINE, EMBASE, Science Citation Index, and the WHO trial search database, supplemented by reference-list searching.
The electronic search was updated in October 2015.
Additional unpublished or incompletely reported data were sought from trial investigators, manufacturers, and the Yale Open Data Access project.
Two reviewers independently screened trials, with a third reviewer resolving disagreements.
Three authors independently extracted outcome data and resolved disagreements by consensus.
For trials reporting multiple treatment periods, the review used data from the longest treatment period.
SGLT2 inhibitor versus placebo and SGLT2 inhibitor versus oral antidiabetic drug comparisons were analyzed separately.
Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane risk-of-bias domains, and certainty of evidence was assessed with GRADE.
Meta-analyses used Review Manager and random-effects models because clinical and methodological heterogeneity was expected.
Continuous outcomes were summarized using mean differences and dichotomous outcomes using risk ratios, both with 95% confidence intervals.
Statistical heterogeneity was evaluated with I-squared and subgroup analyses included individual SGLT2 inhibitors and oral comparator classes.
Small-study effects were assessed when at least ten randomized trials were available, using Egger-type methods for continuous outcomes and Harbord-type methods for dichotomous outcomes.
The review protocol was prospectively registered in PROSPERO as CRD42014008960.
The PRISMA checklist documented reporting against the PRISMA 2009 framework.

The supplementary data-source file grouped multiple publications belonging to the same randomized trial and marked primary reports while documenting additional manufacturer, investigator, and YODA data sources.

The search flow identified 1,087 database records plus 20 records from other sources; after deduplication 780 records were screened, 76 full texts were assessed, and 42 studies (59 reports) entered quantitative synthesis.

Seventeen full-text studies were excluded for reasons including ineligible doses, open-label extensions, chronic kidney disease, unpublished status, unavailable outcome data, nonblinding, combination therapy, or lack of relevant outcomes.

Across included trials, random sequence generation, allocation concealment, and blinding were generally judged at low risk, while other bias remained unclear for all trials because every trial was industry funded.
No included randomized trial was judged at low risk of bias across every assessed domain.
The detailed supplementary characteristics table reports study-level design, populations, interventions, outcomes, and risk-of-bias judgments for the included randomized trials.
The excluded-study supplement documents excluded full-text studies and the review authors’ reasons for exclusion.
SGLT2 inhibitors reduced HbA1c versus placebo by a pooled mean difference of -0.69 percentage points (95% CI -0.75 to -0.62) across 34 RCTs and 9,154 participants.

canonical_statement: GRADE certainty for the primary HbA1c comparison versus placebo was rated low because of heterogeneity and evidence of small-study/publication bias.
The primary HbA1c meta-analysis versus placebo showed substantial heterogeneity (I² approximately 75%) and evidence of small-study effects (P=0.015).
The HbA1c comparison against oral antidiabetic drugs also showed between-study heterogeneity and evidence of small-study effects (P=0.0385).
All included randomized trials were industry funded, leaving other bias unclear and limiting independence of the evidence base.
Serious clinical outcomes were uncommon, producing wide confidence intervals and substantial imprecision for mortality, cancer, severe hypoglycaemia, and cardiovascular events.
Adverse-event reporting was inconsistent across trials, limiting confidence in pooled harm estimates.
The review restricted efficacy comparisons to maximal approved doses and therefore does not characterize all dose-response relationships.
Clinical and statistical heterogeneity was substantial for several efficacy and metabolic outcomes.
Most trials were conducted in research-oriented settings, which the authors identified as a limitation to generalizability.
The evidence base largely predates long-term cardiovascular and renal outcome trials that later became central to SGLT2 inhibitor use.
At maximal approved doses and treatment durations of at least 12 weeks, SGLT2 inhibitors lowered HbA1c compared with placebo and with other oral antidiabetic therapies.
SGLT2 inhibitors were associated with increased urinary and genital tract infections, while the available randomized-trial evidence did not demonstrate an increase in serious adverse events.
The authors concluded that SGLT2 inhibitors may also improve body weight, blood pressure, and HDL cholesterol, but interpretation is constrained by heterogeneity and bias.
The authors called for larger and longer randomized trials with systematic reporting of cardiovascular outcomes, ketoacidosis, severe hypoglycaemia, and renal safety.
The authors reported that the systematic review received no specific funding.

Several authors reported lecture, advisory-board, consulting, or research relationships with pharmaceutical companies; the paper also disclosed consultancy fees to Systematic Research Ltd for Cathy Bennett’s work on the project.
The paper stated that all relevant data were contained within the article and its Supporting Information files.
The authors acknowledged additional trial data supplied by Boehringer Ingelheim and AstraZeneca and data accessed through the Yale Open Data Access project under an agreement with Janssen.

Source inconsistency: the main text reports the serious-adverse-event placebo analysis as 34 RCTs, n=10,703, RR 0.99 (95% CI 0.87–1.12), while S2 Table reports n=11,140 and RR 0.99 (95% CI 0.88–1.13).
Source inconsistency: the main text reports severe hypoglycaemia versus placebo with n=5,077, while S2 Table reports n=5,083 for the same RR 0.75 (95% CI 0.23–2.43).

Source inconsistency: Table 2 reports the pooled fasting-plasma-glucose difference as -28.1 mg/dL, whereas the Results prose reports -0.9 mmol/L for the same pooled comparison; the source does not reconcile these two representations.
Source inconsistency: Table 2 prints the triglyceride 95% CI as -0.16 to +0.02 mmol/L, while the Results prose describes -0.16 to -0.02 mmol/L.
Source inconsistency: cardiovascular-event participant totals differ between the main-text arm counts and S2 Table total.
